title: Your role: training versus competition
summary: In training you are the coach’s voice. In competition coaching is forbidden, so you pass on only what the referee, the jury and the organiser say.

body.html: In training you are the coach’s voice. Pass on each instruction in full, in the coach’s order and tone: firm about safety, warm with praise. Do not soften criticism or add reasons the coach did not give. Do not add technique tips of your own, even when you know the answer. If you missed a word, ask before you translate.

A competition is different. In both Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting, coaching a competitor during the competition is forbidden. The shooter gets a yellow card, repeats bring heavier penalties, and the referee sends the person who coached out of the shooting area (Chapter 8 · No coaching during competition, Chapter 21 · No coaching during competition). The referee’s decision is the referee’s alone. Nobody in the squad comments on hits. Open criticism of a ruling counts as an attempt to influence the referee, that is, trying to push the referee towards another decision (Chapter 11 · What counts as influencing the referee, Chapter 22 · What counts as an attempt to influence).

Here is the honest part: the FITASC rulebooks do not mention interpreters at all. They do not say whether passing on a coach’s advice word for word counts as coaching. Nor do they say where an interpreter may stand. This is an open question for FITASC, so do not present any answer as official.

Until FITASC answers, follow a safe practice. In competition, interpret only what passes between your shooter and the referee, the jury or the organiser: calls, decisions, warnings, protests, times and squad lists. Before the event, tell the referee or organiser who you are and agree where you will stand. If a coach asks you to pass on advice during the competition, decline politely and say why. This protects your shooter from a yellow card.

The rules do not say whether a break between rounds still counts as “during the competition”. If you are unsure, ask the jury or the organiser before you pass on any advice. Where to stand and when to speak: Where to stand and when to speak.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: Tell her she’s lifting her head on the second bird.
phrases.meaning: Training: pass it on fully when the gun is open.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: Quick — tell him to give the crosser more.
phrases.meaning: Competition: this is coaching. Decline politely; do not pass it on.

phrases.speaker: referee
phrases.meaning: The referee asks why you are near the stand; introduce yourself and your role.

phrases.speaker: shooter
phrases.en: Ask the referee if I can still change chokes.
phrases.meaning: A procedural question to the referee: you may interpret it.

key_points.html: Training: the coach’s voice — complete, same tone, nothing of your own
Competition: coaching is forbidden (yellow card, coach removed)
Open FITASC question: rulebooks do not mention interpreters
Safe practice: interpret only referee, jury and organiser communication in competition
Introduce yourself to the referee and agree where you stand

quiz.q: During a competition round the coach asks you to tell the shooter “more lead on the crosser”. What do you do?

options.text: Whisper it quickly while he loads
Pass it on after the next target
Decline politely: that would be coaching
Ask the referee to pass it on

quiz.explain: Coaching during competition is forbidden and the shooter would get a yellow card. The rules do not say whether relaying advice is allowed, so stay on the safe side.

quiz.q: What do the FITASC rulebooks say about interpreters?

options.text: They may stand on the stand
Nothing: it is an open question

quiz.explain: The rulebooks do not mention interpreters, so their exact position in competition is an open question for FITASC.

quiz.q: In training, the coach says “Not bad, but you stopped the gun.” How do you translate?

options.text: Fully and in the same tone, both parts
Only the praise, to keep the guest happy
Only the fault, to save time
Add your own tip on how to fix it

quiz.explain: You neither soften nor inflate: the whole message, in the coach’s tone, with nothing of your own.
